power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p ≥ 0.53", Sentence = "For all other predictors, there was no evidence of differences between subgroups (all adjusted p ≥ 0.53)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Introduction: Atmospheric conditions under climate change constitute an increasing health burden and raise pressure on health care systems.
Intensive care units (ICUs) are particularly vulnerable due to their low buffer capacity and high utilization rates.
This study aimed to examine the association between atmospheric exposures and ICU admissions for intensive care relevant diseases across Germany.
Methods: We analyzed daily time-series data on ICU admissions from AOK health insurances and atmospheric data in the period 2009 to 2023.
Using principal component analysis, we clustered Germany into eleven human-bioclimatic regions.
For each atmospheric predictor, the optimal time lag was selected, and disease-specific predictor sets were defined while accounting for multiple testing.
In each region, we fitted quasi-Poisson generalized additive models to estimate diseasespecific ICU admission risks associated with atmospheric exposures.
Models were stratified by age (<60, ≥60 years) and sex.
text.formatted: Models were stratified by age (<60, ≥60 years) and sex.

text.text: Model performance was assessed using (weighted) explained deviance (WED).
Results: Over the 15-year study period, on average 2,526 ICU admissions per 100,000 AOK insured persons per year were recorded in Germany (44% women, 74.3% aged ≥60 years).
Pressure-related variables were most frequently associated with ICU admissions (p ≤ 0.05).
Sea-level pressure demonstrated a significant association in 29.3% of the models.
Heat-related variables, including tropical nights (18.3%) and summer days (17.8%), were significantly associated with ICU admissions in Germany.
Among air pollutants, ozone showed the highest proportion of significant associations (15.6%).
Significant associations for heat-related atmospheric variables were observed more frequently among men and persons ≥60 years.
Mean model performance across all models was 10% WED.
The models for ICU admissions due to myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) in the East German Lowlands demonstrated the best model performance (WED: 49%).
Discussion: Atmospheric factors were associated with ICU admissions, and these associations differed by region, disease, and age-sex group.
Pressure-and heat-related factors were the most relevant atmospheric factors.
These findings indicate that atmospheric factors have the potential to adversely impact intensive health care preparedness and delivery.
Urbanization, economic development, and industrial growth have contributed to increasing levels of air pollution and changes of the atmospheric environment over recent decades.
At the same time, climate change is expected to increase the frequency, intensity, and duration of atmospheric hazards, including heat waves and other extreme weather events [1, 2].
text.formatted: At the same time, climate change is expected to increase the frequency, intensity, and duration of atmospheric hazards, including heat waves and other extreme weather events <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: These environmental changes represent important stressors for human health and are associated with substantial increases in morbidity and mortality [3, 4].
text.formatted: These environmental changes represent important stressors for human health and are associated with substantial increases in morbidity and mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: A growing body of evidence indicates that there is an influence on the occurrence and exacerbation of a wide range of diseases, including respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurological, and trauma-related diseases [5].
text.formatted: A growing body of evidence indicates that there is an influence on the occurrence and exacerbation of a wide range of diseases, including respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal, neurological, and trauma-related diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: As many of these diseases frequently require hospital-based treatment, climate change-related health impacts are expected to place an increasing burden on health care systems.

Vulnerable populations, particularly older adults, children, and individuals with pre-existing medical conditions, are disproportionately affected by atmospheric hazards and extreme weather events [4, 6].
text.formatted: Vulnerable populations, particularly older adults, children, and individuals with pre-existing medical conditions, are disproportionately affected by atmospheric hazards and extreme weather events <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of atmosphere-health relationships is essential for quantifying future health care demands and supporting the development of climate-resilient health care systems and infrastructure [7].
text.formatted: Consequently, a comprehensive understanding of atmosphere-health relationships is essential for quantifying future health care demands and supporting the development of climate-resilient health care systems and infrastructure <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>.

text.text: Numerous studies have reported associations between atmospheric stressors and increased rates of mortality and hospital admissions [2, 8].
text.formatted: Numerous studies have reported associations between atmospheric stressors and increased rates of mortality and hospital admissions <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: However, considerably less attention has been paid to the potential implications for intensive care medicine, despite intensive care units (ICUs) representing one of the most resource-intensive and capacity-limited sectors of health care.

Patients requiring intensive care are often characterized by severe acute illnesses, multiple comorbidities, and heightened physiological vulnerability, making them particularly susceptible to environmental stressors.
Moreover, ongoing climate change may translate into higher demand for critical care services, potentially exacerbating existing capacity constraints.
In Germany, the average ICU utilization rate of 81.6% leaves limited reserve capacity to accommodate sudden increases in demand associated with atmospheric conditions [9].
text.formatted: In Germany, the average ICU utilization rate of 81.6% leaves limited reserve capacity to accommodate sudden increases in demand associated with atmospheric conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref>.

text.text: This challenge is further intensified by the persistent shortage of specialized healthcare personnel [10].
text.formatted: This challenge is further intensified by the persistent shortage of specialized healthcare personnel <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: Understanding how atmospheric factors are associated with ICU admissions has therefore a substantial clinical and public health relevance, as it may help identify vulnerable patient groups, anticipate future health care demands, and support strategic resource planning in intensive care.

Despite growing evidence on climate-related health effects, nationwide assessments of atmospheric influences on ICU admissions remain limited, particularly regarding regional and disease-specific differences.
This study addresses this gap by linking region-specific daily ICU admissions with atmospheric data across Germany.

The objectives are to analyze atmosphere-ICU associations across Germany, quantify regional heterogeneity, and identify diseases and age-sex-specific subgroups with heightened susceptibility to atmospheric conditions.
Daily time-series data of intensive care admissions derived from anonymized, nationwide routine data from the German health care system was collected for the years 2009-2023.
The effects of the Covid-19 pandemic on ICU admissions were observed, particularly in respiratory diseases (see Supplementary Figure S1).
text.formatted: The effects of the Covid-19 pandemic on ICU admissions were observed, particularly in respiratory diseases (see Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: However, the impact on intensive care as a whole was negligible (Figure 2).
text.formatted: However, the impact on intensive care as a whole was negligible (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: Moreover, a long-term downward trend in admissions and health care utilization has been observed [11].
text.formatted: Moreover, a long-term downward trend in admissions and health care utilization has been observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the pandemic years were not considered separately.
The 15-year health data was provided by the AOK Research Institute (WIdO), derived from statutory health insurance data of eleven regional AOK insurances.
The study sample was stratified by sex and two age groups (<60 and ≥60 years old).
text.formatted: The study sample was stratified by sex and two age groups (<60 and ≥60 years old).

text.text: The choice for only two age groups was motivated by the need to standardize the health insurance-based subsample of about 30% of the population to the total population of Germany in a follow-up study.
Thus, four subgroups were analyzed: female ≥60 years (FE), male ≥60 years (ME), female <60 years (FY), and male <60 years (MY).
text.formatted: Thus, four subgroups were analyzed: female ≥60 years (FE), male ≥60 years (ME), female <60 years (FY), and male <60 years (MY).

text.text: Repeated admissions of one individual were not accounted for.
All admissions were treated as independent admissions.
The operationalization of intensive care required a broader definition, given that not all hospitals have dedicated ICU or fulfil the billing criteria for complex intensive care treatment.

Therefore, the operation and procedure (OPS) code for intensive care complex treatment, the OPS code for intensive care patient monitoring, or the department code of ICU was used as a selection criterion (Supplementary, Table S1& S2).
text.formatted: Therefore, the operation and procedure (OPS) code for intensive care complex treatment, the OPS code for intensive care patient monitoring, or the department code of ICU was used as a selection criterion (Supplementary, Table <ref type="table">S1& S2</ref>).

text.text: The study included admissions of the 13 most common diseases in the ICU, accounting for 46% of all ICU admissions [5, 12, 13].
text.formatted: The study included admissions of the 13 most common diseases in the ICU, accounting for 46% of all ICU admissions <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>.

text.text: The diseases were classified using the codes of the International Statistical Classification Of Diseases And Related Health Problems, 10th revision, German Modification (ICD-10-GM) (Supplementary, Table S3).
text.formatted: The diseases were classified using the codes of the International Statistical Classification Of Diseases And Related Health Problems, 10th revision, German Modification (ICD-10-GM) (Supplementary, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S3</ref>).

text.text: They were grouped into the following categories: cardiovascular diseases (heart failure, non-ST elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI), ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), tachycardia, pulmonary artery embolism), respiratory diseases (pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)), neurological diseases (ischemic insult, transient ischemic attack, non subdural hemorrhage, epilepsy), internal diseases (sepsis) and traumatic diseases (trauma).
For a few disease categories, the term "ICU admissions" was defined more broadly than the ICU definition given above.
For cardiovascular diseases, continuous rhythm monitoring is essential.
Therefore, admissions treated in settings such as chest pain units were also classified as ICU admissions.
Without this adjustment, a considerable proportion of cardiovascular admissions requiring intensive monitoring might not have been captured.

Similarly, for respiratory diseases, admissions receiving ventilation outside of an ICU were included to ensure that all admissions requiring intensive care-level treatment were represented (Supplementary Table S3).
text.formatted: Similarly, for respiratory diseases, admissions receiving ventilation outside of an ICU were included to ensure that all admissions requiring intensive care-level treatment were represented (Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S3</ref>).

text.text: For neurological diseases (except epilepsy), admissions were categorized separately according to whether treatment was provided in an ICU or in a specialized stroke unit (Supplementary, Table S4), resulting in the consideration of 16 outcome types in total.
text.formatted: For neurological diseases (except epilepsy), admissions were categorized separately according to whether treatment was provided in an ICU or in a specialized stroke unit (Supplementary, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S4</ref>), resulting in the consideration of 16 outcome types in total.

text.text: Prior to statistical model building, the daily health data was analyzed regarding erroneous values within the ICD-10-GM coding system, internal validity as well as with respect to completeness, homogeneity, variability, outliers and trends [14, 15].
text.formatted: Prior to statistical model building, the daily health data was analyzed regarding erroneous values within the ICD-10-GM coding system, internal validity as well as with respect to completeness, homogeneity, variability, outliers and trends <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15]</ref>.

text.text: To account for regional differences and to define internally homogeneous exposure clusters, Germany was divided into human-bioclimatic regions (HBC-regions).
The regionalization was based on seasonally resolved climatic variables, which are related to human health.
Data was derived from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset provided by the Copernicus Climate Data Store [16].
text.formatted: Data was derived from the ERA5-Land reanalysis dataset provided by the Copernicus Climate Data Store <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: For the classification of the HBC-regions, a spatial principal component analysis was used to identify the optimal number of regions, and the grid boxes were assigned to the determined number of HBCregions by means of a k-means cluster analysis.
The regionalization identified six main regions and, given the presence of still some noticeable intra-regional variations, three further subregions using the aforementioned methods were built.
Overall, the regionalization resulted in eleven distinct, bioclimatic consistent HBC-regions, characterizing the different human-bioclimatic conditions in Germany on regional scales (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Overall, the regionalization resulted in eleven distinct, bioclimatic consistent HBC-regions, characterizing the different human-bioclimatic conditions in Germany on regional scales (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: The eleven HBC-regions were mapped to their corresponding ZIP codes, allowing the daily health data to be assigned to the respective regions.
For assessing the atmospheric impact on intensive care, daily data of multiple atmospheric variables and indices was collected.

Daily meteorological data was obtained from the quality-controlled ERA5 reanalysis data of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), and air pollution data from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) [16] [17] [18] [19].
text.formatted: Daily meteorological data was obtained from the quality-controlled ERA5 reanalysis data of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), and air pollution data from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: In total, 31 atmospheric variables and indices were extracted (Supplementary, Table S5).
text.formatted: In total, 31 atmospheric variables and indices were extracted (Supplementary, Table <ref type="table">S5</ref>).

text.text: Averaging atmospheric exposures within the HBC-regions inevitably led to a reduction in the spatial resolution of the atmospheric data as well as to a smoothing of extremes.
This limitation particularly affected the representation of urban heat island effects as well as the small-scale variability of air quality variables.
Thus, regional exposure characterization can be regarded as background exposure, giving an overall conservative exposure assignment.

To investigate the associations between daily ICU admissions and atmospheric data, we calculated generalized additive models (GAMs) with quasi-Poisson distribution to account for overdispersion [20, 21].
text.formatted: To investigate the associations between daily ICU admissions and atmospheric data, we calculated generalized additive models (GAMs) with quasi-Poisson distribution to account for overdispersion <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>.

text.text: GAMs are particularly useful for time series analyses that investigate the relationship between climate effects and health, and allow nonparametric adjustments for nonlinear effects [20, [22] [23] [24].
text.formatted: GAMs are particularly useful for time series analyses that investigate the relationship between climate effects and health, and allow nonparametric adjustments for nonlinear effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: In each HBC-region the ICU outcomes stratified according to sex and age were analyzed.
In total, 704 different models (11 regions x 16 ICU outcome types x 4 subgroups) were created to establish the regional associations between the daily ICU admissions and atmospheric factors.

To determine the optimal lag in the exposure-outcome models, for all regions, outcome types and subgroups bivariate predictor-response models were built using no lag up to ten days lag for meteorological predictors and up to seven days for air quality predictors [23, 25].
text.formatted: To determine the optimal lag in the exposure-outcome models, for all regions, outcome types and subgroups bivariate predictor-response models were built using no lag up to ten days lag for meteorological predictors and up to seven days for air quality predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: The optimal lag for each atmospheric predictor was selected based on the relative risk (RR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) [26].
text.formatted: The optimal lag for each atmospheric predictor was selected based on the relative risk (RR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Subsequently, for each region, outcome type and subgroup GAMs were established using all predictor variables with their specific lags.
Predictor variables remained in the models if the pvalue was significant (α ≤ 0.05) after Bonferroni correction.
The correction for multiple testing was applied separately within each region-, outcome-, and subgroup-specific model [27, 28].
text.formatted: The correction for multiple testing was applied separately within each region-, outcome-, and subgroup-specific model <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>.

text.text: In order to harmonize predictor sets according to outcome types and to facilitate interpretation, the final predictor set per outcome type consisted of all predictors which were at least significant in one GAM out of 44 in total (11 regions x 4 subgroups).
The resulting outcome type-specific predictor sets were subsequently used to fit the final GAMs for each combination of outcome type, subgroup, and HBCregion.
For nonlinear associations, thin plate regression splines with shrinkage were used as the smoothing basis [29, 30].
text.formatted: For nonlinear associations, thin plate regression splines with shrinkage were used as the smoothing basis <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref>.

text.text: Models were fitted using restricted maximum likelihood (REML), which provides robust estimation of smoothing parameters and is particularly suitable for models with overdispersed count data [30].
text.formatted: Models were fitted using restricted maximum likelihood (REML), which provides robust estimation of smoothing parameters and is particularly suitable for models with overdispersed count data <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: The shrinkage approach (select = TRUE) additionally allowed terms with little explanatory value to be penalized towards zero, thereby reducing the influence of irrelevant predictors [30].
text.formatted: The shrinkage approach (select = TRUE) additionally allowed terms with little explanatory value to be penalized towards zero, thereby reducing the influence of irrelevant predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Next to atmospheric predictors, the models controlled for seasonality effects through sinusoidal and cosinusoidal components, time trend as well as weekday versus weekend [26, [31] [32] [33] [34].
text.formatted: Next to atmospheric predictors, the models controlled for seasonality effects through sinusoidal and cosinusoidal components, time trend as well as weekday versus weekend <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: Seasonality and time trend were represented in the models using thin plate regression splines.
Collinearity among the atmospheric predictors was assessed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.
Predictor pairs with an absolute correlation coefficient of |ρ| ≥ 0.7 were considered as collinear.

In cases of collinearity, the predictor showing the stronger statistical association with the respective outcome, as indicated by the lower p-value in the regression analysis, was retained, while the less strongly associated predictor was excluded from the model [35].
text.formatted: In cases of collinearity, the predictor showing the stronger statistical association with the respective outcome, as indicated by the lower p-value in the regression analysis, was retained, while the less strongly associated predictor was excluded from the model <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: Explained deviance (ED) was used to check model performance.

To summarize subgroup-specific performance for each region and outcome type, weighted explained deviance (WED) was calculated by weighting the EDs of the subgroups according to their proportion in the case numbers of a region and outcome.
Differences between subgroups were assessed descriptively by comparing the WED, ED and the proportion of atmospheric predictors with a significant association (p ≤ 0.05).
These comparisons are therefore exploratory and do not allow conclusions on statistically significant differences between subgroups.
For the regional outcome type with the highest WED, predictor-specific log-RRs from the corresponding subgroup-specific models were compared assuming independence between subgroups.
Heterogeneity across the four subgroups was assessed using Cochran's Q test and quantified by I².
The resulting p-values were adjusted across predictors using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure [36].
text.formatted: The resulting p-values were adjusted across predictors using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>.

text.text: For predictors exhibiting significant heterogeneity (adjusted p < 0.05), pairwise z-tests were performed, comparing sexes within age groups and age groups within sexes.
text.formatted: For predictors exhibiting significant heterogeneity (adjusted p < 0.05), pairwise z-tests were performed, comparing sexes within age groups and age groups within sexes.

text.text: Results are reported as ratios of RRs with corresponding 95% CIs and p-values.
The main statistical analyses were performed using the package mgcv in R (Version 4.5.1) and RStudio (Version 2025.05.1.513) [20, 23].
text.formatted: The main statistical analyses were performed using the package mgcv in R (Version 4.5.1) and RStudio (Version 2025.05.1.513) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: The study was conducted in accordance to the Declaration of Helsinki and the reporting follows the RECORD guidelines for studies using routine health data [37].
text.formatted: The study was conducted in accordance to the Declaration of Helsinki and the reporting follows the RECORD guidelines for studies using routine health data <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: The sample comprised on average 2,526 standardized ICU admissions per 100,000 AOK insured persons per year over the 15-year study period (a total of 9,970,548 ICU admissions) (Figure 2, Supplementary: Standardized ICU admissions per outcome type, Figure S1). 44% of the admissions were female and 74.3% of the admitted persons were ≥60 years old.
text.formatted: The sample comprised on average 2,526 standardized ICU admissions per 100,000 AOK insured persons per year over the 15-year study period (a total of 9,970,548 ICU admissions) (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>, Supplementary: Standardized ICU admissions per outcome type, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>). 44% of the admissions were female and 74.3% of the admitted persons were ≥60 years old.

text.text: ICU admissions were most frequent in the ME subgroup and least frequent in the FY subgroup.
Compared with the FY subgroup, the ME subgroup exhibited approximately three times as many ventilation days.
In contrast, obesity was more common among people younger than 60 years than among those aged ≥60 years.
The highest proportion of obese people was observed in the FY subgroup (Table 1).
text.formatted: The highest proportion of obese people was observed in the FY subgroup (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: Trauma accounted for the highest number of ICU admissions among all outcome types.
In the ≥60 year subgroups, ischemic stroke represented one of the most frequent outcome types, whereas pneumonia was more prevalent in the <60 year subgroups (Table 1).
text.formatted: In the ≥60 year subgroups, ischemic stroke represented one of the most frequent outcome types, whereas pneumonia was more prevalent in the <60 year subgroups (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: An almost continuous decrease in ICU admissions was observed across all HBC-regions (except 6.3) from 2017 onwards.
Over the entire study period, HBC-region 6.1 (Mecklenburg Lake District in northeastern Germany) consistently showed the highest ICU admission rate per 100,000 AOK insured people (Figure 2).
text.formatted: Over the entire study period, HBC-region 6.1 (Mecklenburg Lake District in northeastern Germany) consistently showed the highest ICU admission rate per 100,000 AOK insured people (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: A comparison of regional atmospheric characteristics revealed pronounced differences across the eleven HBC-regions (Supplementary Figures S2-S8).
text.formatted: A comparison of regional atmospheric characteristics revealed pronounced differences across the eleven HBC-regions (Supplementary Figures <ref type="figure">S2-S8</ref>).

text.text: Distinct regional patterns emerged, particularly regarding cold exposure, heat exposure, and air pollution.
The most cold-exposed regions were observed in HBC-regions 5.2 (Thuringian-Franconian Low Mountain Range) and 3.1 (Alpine Foothills & Southern Low Mountain Ranges).
text.formatted: The most cold-exposed regions were observed in HBC-regions 5.2 (Thuringian-Franconian Low Mountain Range) and 3.1 (Alpine Foothills & Southern Low Mountain Ranges).

text.text: HBC-region 5.2 exhibited the highest number of ice days (average: 27 days/year; daily Tmax < 0°C) and the lowest mean wind chill index (WCI, mean ± standard deviation: 5.4 ± 7.4°C).
text.formatted: HBC-region 5.2 exhibited the highest number of ice days (average: 27 days/year; daily Tmax < 0°C) and the lowest mean wind chill index (WCI, mean ± standard deviation: 5.4 ± 7.4°C).

text.text: Similarly, HBC-region 3.1 showed pronounced cold exposure, with the highest number of frost days (average: 95.2 days/year; daily Tmin < 0°C) and an absence of tropical nights (daily Tmin > 20°C).
text.formatted: Similarly, HBC-region 3.1 showed pronounced cold exposure, with the highest number of frost days (average: 95.2 days/year; daily Tmin < 0°C) and an absence of tropical nights (daily Tmin > 20°C).

text.text: In contrast, HBC-region 2.2 (southwest Germany) represented the most heat-exposed region, with the highest number of tropical nights (average: 1.5 nights/year, maximum: 6 nights in 2018), summer days (average: 43.5 days/year; daily Tmax > 25°C), and hot days (average: 9.6 days/year; daily Tmax > 30°C), as well as the highest mean wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT: 13.6 ± 7.5°C).
text.formatted: In contrast, HBC-region 2.2 (southwest Germany) represented the most heat-exposed region, with the highest number of tropical nights (average: 1.5 nights/year, maximum: 6 nights in 2018), summer days (average: 43.5 days/year; daily Tmax > 25°C), and hot days (average: 9.6 days/year; daily Tmax > 30°C), as well as the highest mean wet-bulb globe temperature (WBGT: 13.6 ± 7.5°C).

text.text: The highest daily mean temperature was observed in HBCregion 1.2 (10.7 ± 6.8°C).
Overall, the air quality in Germany improved over the study period.
Only ozone levels continued to rise in all regions over the 15 years (Supplementary, Figure S2).
text.formatted: Only ozone levels continued to rise in all regions over the 15 years (Supplementary, Figure <ref type="figure">S2</ref>).

text.text: Even though the air pollution exposure on the chosen regional scale does only reflect average background conditions, distinct air pollution characteristics could be noticed.
Elevated air pollutant concentrations were primarily observed in Lower Rhine and southwest Germany (HBC-regions 1.2, 2.2).

The Lower Rhine region exhibited the highest daily mean concentrations of nitrogen dioxide (NO₂) (8.2 ± 3.7ppbv) and particulate matter (PM10) (19.5 ± 6.6µg/m³), while southwest Germany showed the highest daily mean PM2.5 concentration (13.5 ± 6.5µg/m³).
In contrast, the highest daily mean ozone concentration was observed in HBC-region 5.2 (36.8 ± 12.4ppbv).

Northern regions exhibited the greatest exposure to atmospheric pressure variability, with HBC-regions 4.1 and 6.3 experiencing the highest frequency of day-to-day pressure changes exceeding 10hPa (approximately 15 days per year).
Likewise, the greatest number of wind days was recorded in north-eastern Germany, particularly in HBC-regions 6.2, 4.1, and 1.1, with up to 18 wind days annually.
Conversely, the highest mean sea-level pressure (SLP) was observed in southern Germany, namely in HBC-regions 3.1 (1017.4hPa) and 2.1 (1017.2hPa).

text.text: Across all models, the three pressure-related variables (SLP, SLPD, wind day) showed most frequently statistically significant associations (p ≤ 0.05) with ICU admissions.
SLP was significantly associated with ICU admissions in 29.3% of all models (206/704 models), wind day in 24.9% (175/704 models) and sea-level pressure difference (SLPD) in 20.2% (142/704 models).
Heat-related predictors followed, in particular tropical nights (18.3% of models) and summer days (17.8%).
Among air pollutants, ozone showed the highest proportion of significant associations (15.6% of models).
Cold wave day was the only atmospheric predictor with no significant association in any model.

text.text: Tests for heterogeneity between subgroups indicated differences only for SLP (Cochran's Q = 14.2, adjusted p = 0.016; I² = 79%).
For all other predictors, there was no evidence of differences between subgroups (all adjusted p ≥ 0.53).

The heterogeneity for SLP was driven by a weaker association in women <60 years compared with men <60 years (ratio of RRs 0.985, 95% CI 0.972 -0.998, p = 0.05) and women ≥60 years (ratio of RRs 0.989, 95%CI 0.980 -0.998, p = 0.05).

text.text: In summary, lower SLP and cold-related conditions were associated with higher risk for NSTEMIrelated ICU admissions in eastern Germany, whereas heat and air pollution showed little or no association.
The present study indicates that atmospheric factors are associated with intensive care admissions, with pronounced differences by atmospheric predictor, outcome, region, age and sex.
Pressurerelated variables were most frequently significantly associated with ICU admissions, followed by heat-related predictors.
Associations were dependent on outcome types and no atmospheric factor was associated with all outcome types.
This suggests that diseases are influenced by different atmospheric exposures.

The relevance of atmospheric pressure for an increased risk of cardiovascular and neurological diseases was also reported in earlier studies showing for example that drops in atmospheric pressure are related with stroke incidence [38] [39] [40].
text.formatted: The relevance of atmospheric pressure for an increased risk of cardiovascular and neurological diseases was also reported in earlier studies showing for example that drops in atmospheric pressure are related with stroke incidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>.

text.text: Heat-related predictors, particularly tropical nights and summer days, were significantly associated with ICU admissions in a considerable proportion of models and were mainly linked to neurological outcomes.
This is consistent with previous research.
He et al. [41] reported that higher nighttime temperatures were associated with an increased stroke risk, and other studies have linked temperature to mortality and cardiopulmonary diseases [4, 42].
text.formatted: He et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref> reported that higher nighttime temperatures were associated with an increased stroke risk, and other studies have linked temperature to mortality and cardiopulmonary diseases <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">42]</ref>.

text.text: The relevance of both day-and nighttime heat for ICU admissions suggests that insufficient nocturnal cooling may contribute to thermal stress.
In contrast, heat and cold (stress) wave related indices were less frequently associated with ICU admissions.

Although earlier studies have reported associations between heat waves and various diseases, inconsistent definitions of spell-based indices and differences in the health outcomes studied make comparisons difficult [12, 43].
text.formatted: Although earlier studies have reported associations between heat waves and various diseases, inconsistent definitions of spell-based indices and differences in the health outcomes studied make comparisons difficult <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43]</ref>.

text.text: Thermo-physiological indices, which combine temperature, humidity and radiation, played an important role in many models.
This supports the assumption that other thermal stress variables than temperature alone are relevant for ICU admissions in Germany.
Also the German Weather Service uses perceived temperature to assess thermal stress and issues warnings to health authorities [44].
text.formatted: Also the German Weather Service uses perceived temperature to assess thermal stress and issues warnings to health authorities <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>.

text.text: Beyond purely temperature-based predictors, thermo-physiological indices should therefore be considered in practical applications to describe thermal stress more accurately.
Among the air pollutants, ozone showed the highest proportion of significant associations with ICU admissions, whereas all other pollutants were significantly associated in fewer than 10 % of models.

A possible explanation is the decline in concentrations of these pollutants over the 15-year study period, which reduced exposure and thus the ability to detect associations, whereas ozone exposure has steadily increased in Germany.
Therefore, future studies and health adaptation tools should consider daily ozone levels to reduce health consequences and support the planning of health care capacities [45].
text.formatted: Therefore, future studies and health adaptation tools should consider daily ozone levels to reduce health consequences and support the planning of health care capacities <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref>.

text.text: However, it also must be noted, that in the present study air pollution exposure was described by regional averages.
This could have led to an exposure underestimation in certain areas such as larger urban areas and industrial hubs.
In the sex-stratified analyses, a larger proportion of models for males showed significant associations with atmospheric factors than for females.

However, since models were fitted separately for each subgroup and comparisons are based on the proportion of significant results, these differences do not necessarily reflect true differences in susceptibility.
Although slightly more ICU admissions occurred among men (56 %), which may have contributed to higher statistical power, this is unlikely to be the sole explanation.

Heat-related factors were more frequently significantly associated with ICU admissions in men, whereas women showed more significant associations with air pollutants, particularly PM10 and ozone, which is in line with literature describing a higher vulnerability of women to air pollution [46].
text.formatted: Heat-related factors were more frequently significantly associated with ICU admissions in men, whereas women showed more significant associations with air pollutants, particularly PM10 and ozone, which is in line with literature describing a higher vulnerability of women to air pollution <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>.

text.text: The lower number of significant heat associations in women could be related to behavioral and occupational factors, such as higher health awareness, greater use of preventive care or lower occupational heat exposure [47, 48].
text.formatted: The lower number of significant heat associations in women could be related to behavioral and occupational factors, such as higher health awareness, greater use of preventive care or lower occupational heat exposure <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">48]</ref>.

text.text: As these factors were not assessed in this study, this explanation remains speculative.
Age-specific analyses showed more significant associations with atmospheric factors in people aged ≥60 years.
Gronlund et al. [49] reported increased hospital admissions and emergency room visits among older people during extreme heat and heatwaves.
text.formatted: Gronlund et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref> reported increased hospital admissions and emergency room visits among older people during extreme heat and heatwaves.

text.text: The higher statistical power of the models for elderly may partly be explained by the high proportion of older adults admitted to ICUs.
Nevertheless, heat-related factors were also significantly associated with ICU admissions in younger age groups, indicating that heat is relevant across all ages.
Overall, the best model performance based on WED was observed for myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) models.
As NSTEMI was among the outcomes with the most frequent ICU admissions, the large number of admissions may have allowed higher statistical power.
In eastern Germany (HBC-region 6.2), atmospheric pressure was significantly associated with NSTEMI ICU admissions in most subgroup models.
A 10hPa drop in atmospheric pressure as well as cold-related events were associated with an increase in ICU admission risk.
In this context, a sudden atmospheric pressure drop may act directly on the cardiovascular system or serve as a proxy for the associated changes of the weather conditions.
For cold-related associations, increased blood viscosity and arterial pressure have been discussed as possible mechanisms, although neither was assessed in this study [50].
text.formatted: For cold-related associations, increased blood viscosity and arterial pressure have been discussed as possible mechanisms, although neither was assessed in this study <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>.

text.text: No clear association was found between heat and NSTEMI, which may be explained by less heat exposure in this region.
The apparently protective effect of heat waves in older men was only marginally significant (upper confidence limit close to 1).
It should therefore be interpreted with caution.
Fine particulate matter has previously been linked to vascular damage and myocardial infarction [51].
text.formatted: Fine particulate matter has previously been linked to vascular damage and myocardial infarction <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref>.

text.text: The absence of such an association in these models may be due to the use of regional averages, which cannot capture small-scale variations in air pollutant concentrations and may therefore obscure localized exposure effects.

Although the effects of the atmospheric factors were relatively small and their public health relevance at the population level is therefore limited, even small changes in ICU admissions can be detrimental to health care preparedness and delivery [52].
text.formatted: Although the effects of the atmospheric factors were relatively small and their public health relevance at the population level is therefore limited, even small changes in ICU admissions can be detrimental to health care preparedness and delivery <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref>.

text.text: A strength of this study is the use of routine data, which reflect real-world healthcare provision and provide a large number of cases, enabling disease-specific and subgroup analyses [14].
text.formatted: A strength of this study is the use of routine data, which reflect real-world healthcare provision and provide a large number of cases, enabling disease-specific and subgroup analyses <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Changes in ICD-10-GM coding were checked and incorporated into the case selection, and the ICU-relevant diseases were defined a priori.
Furthermore, the consideration of different HBC-regions in Germany made it possible to capture regional differences in atmospheric-health associations across the whole country.
Several limitations should be considered.
AOK data are claims data, and coding biases due to financial incentives may have affected data validity [14].
text.formatted: AOK data are claims data, and coding biases due to financial incentives may have affected data validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Also, the sample consisted exclusively of AOK insured individuals.
The age and sex structure differs from that of the German population, which may limit external validity.
However, AOK insured people account for almost one third of the German population [53].
text.formatted: However, AOK insured people account for almost one third of the German population <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref>.

text.text: In a follow-up study, which will assess the prediction suitability of the models, the results will be age-sex standardized to the German population.
Thus, subgroup models were fitted separately in the present study, taking the loss that differences in the number of ICU admissions may have led to differences in statistical power.
Regarding atmospheric predictors, the use of regional averages for exposure did not allow to capture small-scale variations, particularly relevant for air pollutants and the urban heat islands.

Furthermore, Bonferroni correction was applied within each model but not across the large number of region-, outcome-and subgroup-specific models, so some significant associations may be chance findings.
Collinear predictors (|ρ| ≥ 0.7) were handled by retaining the predictor with the lower p-value in the regional regression analysis.
As a result, retained predictors may be favored, which should be considered when interpreting the proportion of significant models and comparing predictors.
Also, as for any epidemiological time series study, the present study does not per se allow causal interpretation.

Models were adjusted for seasonality, time trend and weekday, but not for other time-varying factors such as public holidays or influenza epidemics, which may be particularly relevant for respiratory outcomes.

The study period of 15 years included the COVID-19 pandemic, as the impact of the pandemic on the intensive care was negligible and the data shown a long-term downward trend in admissions, suggesting a lasting change in health care structures [11].
text.formatted: The study period of 15 years included the COVID-19 pandemic, as the impact of the pandemic on the intensive care was negligible and the data shown a long-term downward trend in admissions, suggesting a lasting change in health care structures <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, given that intensive care constitutes critical infrastructure that is less affected by the postponement of elective procedures than general hospital admissions, the pandemic period was not analyzed separately [54].
text.formatted: Furthermore, given that intensive care constitutes critical infrastructure that is less affected by the postponement of elective procedures than general hospital admissions, the pandemic period was not analyzed separately <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref>.

text.text: In conclusion, this study indicates that atmospheric factors, most noticeably pressure-related ones, are associated with intensive care admissions in Germany.
The study also extends previous research that focused mainly on mortality and general hospitalization.
Associations differed by region, outcome, age and sex.
Although the observed effects were small, they may be relevant for critical health care infrastructure such as intensive care and may inform regional ICU capacity planning.
In a follow-up study, the identified associations will be used to assess short-term predictability of ICU admissions with the scope to develop a practically relevant tool.
